title: When Should LLMs Be Less Specific? Selective Abstraction for Reliable Long-Form Text Generation
claim: Binary abstention and claim removal discard useful content; replacing uncertain details with less specific but reliable ones gives a better risk-coverage trade-off.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: three-way contrast, worked example chain, risk-coverage plot
description: Three panels read left to right. The left panel starts with a yellow 'Uncertain atom' card ('Amelia Earhart was born in Chicago, Illinois', confidence 70%, marked with a red X). Three arrows lead from it to three colored boxes. A red 'Abstain' box shows a big T glyph and 'discard whole answer'. An orange 'Redact' box shows struck-through text and 'remove atom'. A teal 'Selective Abstraction' box shows 'Amelia Earhart was born in the US' with a green check and 'trade specificity for reliability'. The middle panel is a vertical chain of rounded cards. Each card holds a claim that gets less specific (Chicago, Illinois → Illinois → Midwestern US → the US). Each carries a confidence badge that rises from 70% to 95%, with red X or green check marks, and ends in an Abstain octagon. The right panel is a risk (%) versus coverage (%) line plot. Atom-wise SA, a blue line, sits below the orange Redaction line and other baselines, shown with markers and a legend.
caption: Left: When facing uncertainty, abstention discards the full answer, redaction removes the atom, and selective abstraction trades specificity for reliability. Middle: Example abstraction sequence of atom-wise SA. Right: Risk-coverage curve on FactScore for gpt-oss-120b. Atom-wise SA achieves lower risk than competitive baselines across the coverage range.
abstract: LLMs are widely used, yet they remain prone to factual errors that erode trust and limit adoption in high-risk settings. One approach to mitigate this risk is to equip models with uncertainty estimation mechanisms that abstain when confidence is low. However, this binary "all-or-nothing" approach is excessively restrictive in long-form settings, often discarding valuable information. We introduce Selective Abstraction (SA), a framework that enables LLMs to trade specificity for reliability by selectively reducing the detail of uncertain content. We formalize SA through selective risk and coverage, and propose Atom-wise Selective Abstraction, a claim-level instantiation that decomposes responses into atomic claims and replaces uncertain atoms with higher-confidence, less specific abstractions. We develop a novel end-to-end pipeline for evaluating long-form generation that instantiates risk as factual correctness and measures coverage as retained information. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation across five LLMs and two long-form factual benchmarks shows that atom-wise SA consistently improves the risk-coverage trade-off, outperforming seven baselines, including claim removal, self-revision, sampling-based aggregation, and chain-of-verification. It improves AURC by up to 35.61% over claim removal, demonstrating that reducing specificity boosts reliability while preserving substantial information. We further provide a risk-guided procedure for selecting a confidence threshold that satisfies a target risk.
